title: Introducing Kimi K3.1 Pro on Amazon Bedrock
abstract: Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed from Moonshot AI is now available on Amazon Bedrock . Part of Moonshot AI’s new K3.1 series, it’s a post-trained version of Kimi K3 with the same 3T-class open-weight architecture and 1-million-token context window, trained with substantially more post-training compute. According to Moonshot AI, that extra training targets long-horizon agentic work and fewer factual errors. It also improves professional tasks such as financial modeling and office documents, and coding for game engines, 3D scenes, and computer-aided design (CAD) scripts. Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed generates output tokens at a higher rate and Moonshot AI reports 2–3 times the speed of Kimi K3.1 Pro. Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed uses the same endpoint, APIs, and features as Kimi K3 on Amazon Bedrock. If you already build with Kimi K3, you can try it by changing the model ID in your existing code. Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed supports tool calling, structured output, configurable reasoning, image input, and streaming. You can adopt Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed without changing your security posture. Your data is processed within the AWS data boundary, isn’t shared with Moonshot AI, and isn’t used to train the model. Zero data retention is always enabled for inference requests, and with zero operator access, AWS operators can’t view your prompts and completions during inference. In this post, we show you how to get started with Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed on Amazon Bedrock. We also cover how to lower costs with the Flex tier, explicit prompt caching for repeated context, and how to use the model as a coding assistant in OpenCode. Get started with Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed on Amazon Bedrock To try the model without writing code, open the Amazon Bedrock console , choose Test , then Playground , and select Kimi K3.1 . From code, Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed is available on the bedrock-runtime endpoint through the OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions and Responses APIs, and through the Amazon Bedrock Converse and Invoke APIs. We recommend the Chat Completions API. You reach the model through cross-Region inference profiles: global.moonshotai.kimi-k3.1 routes requests to any supported commercial AWS Region, and costs less per token than the geographic profiles. We recommend it for most workloads. us.moonshotai.kimi-k3.1 keeps processing within US Regions, and in.moonshotai.kimi-k3.1 keeps it within India Regions, for workloads with data residency requirements. Prerequisites To follow the examples, you need: An AWS account with access to Amazon Bedrock. Python 3.11 or later, with the OpenAI SDK , aws-bedrock-token-generator , and boto3 installed ( pip install -U openai aws-bedrock-token-generator boto3 ). An AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) identity allowed to call bedrock:InvokeModel and bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream on the Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed inference profiles. Add bedrock:CallWithBearerToken if you authenticate with a bearer token. Call Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed with the Chat Completions API If your application already uses the OpenAI SDK, point it at the Amazon Bedrock endpoint and change the model name. The following example creates a short-term bearer token from your AWS credentials and sends one request: from openai import OpenAI from aws_bedrock_token_generator import provide_token REGION = "us-west-2" MODEL_ID = "global.moonshotai.kimi-k3.1" # A short-term token derived from your AWS credentials, so no long-lived key is stored in code client = OpenAI( base_url=f"https://bedrock-runtime.{REGION}.amazonaws.com/openai/v1", api_key=provide_token(region=REGION), ) completion = client.chat.completions.create( model=MODEL_ID, messages=[ {"role": "system", "content": "You are a concise senior engineer."}, {"role": "user", "content": "When should I prefer a queue over a stream?"}, ], reasoning_effort="high", ) print(completion.choices[0].message.content) Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed always reasons before it answers. title: Build a daily dependency watcher with LangGraph and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore web search
abstract: AI agents increasingly handle work that depends on what changed today, such as security advisories, product releases, prices, and regulations. A model’s training data can’t answer those questions, so agents need web search. For production use, teams also need results they can cite, and control over which sources count. They want search queries to stay inside their cloud environment because those queries often reveal internal work. The Web Search API in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is now available. It gives agents and applications current web results through a single API call, signed with the AWS credentials they already use. AWS serves every query from a web index that Amazon operates, and doesn’t send it to a third-party search engine. Each result includes the page’s title, URL, publication date, and an extract relevant to the query. Requests can include or exclude domains, and limit results to a publication date range. On AWS Lambda , Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) , or Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime , your agent calls the API with its execution role. There’s no search API key to store or rotate. Web Search on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is also available through AgentCore Gateway , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. There, one administrator source policy covers every agent and Model Context Protocol (MCP) client. For LangChain developers, the AgentCore web search tool in LangChain’s AWS integration now calls the Web Search API. One function call gives an agent current, cited search results. The tool can also hold rules that the model can’t change, such as a date window, a source blocklist, and a search budget. It returns its results as data that your code can check. It works with LangChain agents, with LangGraph , the orchestration framework that runs them, and with Deep Agents , which adds subagents, a virtual filesystem, and context compression. In this post, you build a daily dependency watch for a security team as a LangGraph graph on the Web Search API. Every morning, the watch checks whether anything new affects the open source packages and container base images the team ships. It researches three package ecosystems in parallel, while your code keeps the date window, the blocklist, and the search budget out of the model’s control. It checks each finding against the sources it cites and remembers what it already reported. Then you run the watch on AgentCore runtime, and offer it across teams through AgentCore Gateway. In our test, the three branches finished in 36 seconds, against 99 seconds one after another. Solution overview The model decides what to search for and writes the findings. Every rule that must hold, whatever the model does, stays in code: the date window, the blocklist, the search budget, and the checks on each finding. Figure 1 shows how these parts fit together when you run the watch from the notebook. Figure 1: A daily dependency watch with LangGraph and the Web Search API, run from a notebook The numbered steps: A run starts the graph with the watchlist and the watch window. fan_out starts one research branch per ecosystem: npm, PyPI, and container base images. LangGraph runs the three branches in parallel. Inside each branch, the agent calls an Anthropic Claude model in Amazon Bedrock . The model decides what to search for and, at the end, produces structured findings. The branch’s search tool adds the date window and the blocklist to each query. It calls the Web Search API with a request signed with AWS Signature Version 4 (SigV4) . Steps 3 and 4 repeat, up to four searches per branch, in every branch at the same time. Each branch keeps only findings that its sources support and that fall inside the window. When all three branches finish, LangGraph merges their findings and runs keep_new once. keep_new checks the LangGraph store and records new findings, so nothing is reported twice. report builds the cited table of new findings for the security team. title: The agent evaluation playbook: Built-in, DeepEval, and AutoEval on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations
abstract: When you deploy an agent to production, one of the hardest questions is whether it’s actually working? The bar isn’t whether it runs. It’s whether it does what the business needs, at scale. Many teams will tell you they can’t really see this. They spot-check outputs, watch latency, and collect user feedback when they can get it. None of that tells you whether the agent finished the user’s task, stayed on topic across a long session, leaked personally identifiable information (PII), or quietly skipped half the steps it was supposed to follow. Figure 1: Teams usually watch surface signals, but business outcomes are decided by the agent behaviors below the waterline Agent evaluation solves this problem. What makes this challenging is that a good score on one metric can hide a failure on another. A support agent can resolve every ticket and still expose personal information in its replies. In this case, the agent is failing although it has a high completion rate. To get evaluation right, measure the behaviors that matter for each agent, at the right level of detail. This post shows how to do this on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. We use the AgentCore built-in evaluators together with the DeepEval and AutoEval evaluators directly from AgentCore Evaluations. Start with business outcomes, instead of metric names The most common mistake is to start with the metric list and pick the names that sound right. “Helpfulness sounds good, so we use it.” The result runs and produces numbers, but it gives almost no useful insight. The metric fits its label, not what success means for the agent. Instead, start with three steps. Define success in business terms. For a customer support agent, that might be first-contact resolution. For a research agent, it might be producing a complete, well-sourced answer grounded entirely in retrieved documents. For a content moderation assistant, it means flagging everything that should be flagged and only what should be flagged. Break the outcome into observable behaviors. A customer support agent that achieves first-contact resolution will typically complete the user’s stated goal, stay coherent across turns when the issue requires clarification, keep responses within compliance boundaries, and correctly invoke backend tools like ticket creation or order lookup. Map each behavior to an evaluator at the right level. Trace-level metrics cover per-turn or per-tool-call behaviors. Session-level metrics cover outcomes that only make sense when you look at the whole conversation. Figure 2: Translating a business outcome into observable behaviors and then into specific evaluators at the trace or session level This three-step process is the mental model that makes evaluation useful. The rest of this post is about what AgentCore gives you to execute it. The evaluator catalog AgentCore has a broad catalog of evaluators from three sources: Built-in evaluators are authored and quality-tested by AWS. You reference them by their ID ( Builtin.GoalSuccessRate , Builtin.Helpfulness , and 13 more) and the service handles everything else. They are benchmarked for reliability and cover the common dimensions, so they are the straightforward place to start. Third-party managed evaluators come from DeepEval and AutoEval , two established open-source evaluation libraries. When you use them in managed mode, AgentCore hosts the code, picks the judge model, and runs inference on its own capacity, exactly like built-in evaluators. If your team already uses one of these libraries in development, you can run the same metrics in production without a separate evaluation service. Custom evaluators take a built-in or third-party evaluator as a base, so you can swap in your own model and modify the prompt or rubric. Figure 3: The three evaluator tiers trade AWS quality assurance for increasing control over the model and account that run inference After creation, a custom derived evaluator is used exactly like other ones. title: Autonomous treasury agents: How Trovata built an AI-native solution on Amazon Bedrock and AgentCore
abstract: Corporate treasury teams face a persistent challenge: fragmented banking data scattered across dozens of bank portals, manual reporting trapped in spreadsheets, and legacy Treasury Management Systems (TMS) that can’t scale for modern enterprise needs. For treasury teams these manual processes create delays, errors, and an inability to make real-time cash decisions when they matter most. Trovata is an AI-native cash and liquidity management platform with direct connections to over 10,000 banks, serving enterprises globally from a single cloud-based platform. In 2023, Trovata launched the first generative AI built specifically for treasury. Now, with Trovata’s latest AI-native updates, they’ve evolved from delivering insights to deploying autonomous agents that act on behalf of treasury teams. Trovata’s customers have seen measurable results: $1M+ in annualized cost savings, over 5 hours per day saved per accounting team, a 77 percent reduction in annual TMS costs, and treasury reporting reduced from hours or days to under a minute. In this post, we explore how Trovata built autonomous treasury agents on Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, the architecture secured with role-based access control (RBAC) that supports bank-branded AI deployment, and how agentic workflows are transforming corporate treasury from manual operations to real-time decision-making at enterprise scale. Solution overview Trovata operates as an AI-native treasury operating system, providing direct connections to over 10,000 banks through a single system for cash reporting, forecasting, analysis, and money movement. Treasury teams today face a three-pressure problem: Fragmented banking data across multiple portals, requiring manual aggregation and reconciliation. Manual reporting and reconciliation consuming hours or even days of skilled team members’ time. Legacy TMS applications that lack cloud-native architecture and AI capabilities needed for modern operations. Trovata’s evolution from its first generative AI for treasury in 2023 to its AI-native capabilities with autonomous agents represents a fundamental shift. The solution moves from static insights to persistent agentic workflows that operate continuously on behalf of treasury teams. Critically, Trovata AI is built directly into the treasury operating system. It’s not a generic chatbot layered on top, but embedded intelligence tied to real treasury objects with a governed path to automation through agents. Trovata chose AWS for this transformation for three reasons. Its serverless, cloud-native infrastructure supports real-time execution, Amazon Bedrock provides large language model (LLM) inference for natural language queries and AI features, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore handles agent orchestration with RBAC security, rapid deployment, and global scale. The core AWS services powering Trovata’s AI-native solution include: Amazon Bedrock – LLM inference for natural language understanding and generation. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore – Agent orchestration, agentic workflows, and RBAC security. Serverless AWS infrastructure – Real-time execution at enterprise scale. Architecture diagram The Trovata AI architecture centers on autonomous treasury agents operating within a bank-branded, RBAC-secured framework. The solution comprises several key components working together: Trovata AI Chat – Natural language querying of multi-bank treasury data, so users can ask questions like “What was our net cash position across all accounts yesterday?” and receive instant, accurate responses. AI Insights – Automated anomaly detection, variance explanation, and trend analysis that surfaces critical information proactively. AI Agents – Persistent workflows running on schedules, triggers, or rules to monitor activity, explain variance, detect anomalies, and deliver updates automatically, without human intervention. title: How TCS built an agentic test orchestrator with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
abstract: This post was co-written with Varun Valsan from Tata Consultancy Services (TCS). Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) runs large-scale testing for Banking, Financial Services, and Insurance (BFSI) clients, where the slowest part of a release is rarely writing application code. The larger constraint is the chain of work that follows: interpreting requirements, designing scenarios, writing and maintaining automation, preparing execution environments, investigating failures, and assembling evidence for review. BFSI clients need to increase testing throughput while preserving the controls expected in financial services. The objective wasn’t to replace quality engineers. It was to remove repetitive translation and execution work so that engineers could spend more time on risk analysis, exploratory testing, and release decisions. These industry needs generated four specific requirements for TCS. First, every test must be grounded in project-specific context rather than generic prompts. Second, it had to cover both API and browser-based UI testing to match how BFSI applications are built. Third, security is paramount, so every tenant’s data and knowledge store must be isolated. Finally, it must provide a repeatable path from requirement ingestion to test evidence and reporting, so the gains hold across teams and releases. In this post, we show how TCS built an agentic test orchestrator that turns requirements into executable, governed tests, and what it changed for its BFSI testing teams. Why conventional automation and systems weren’t enough TCS already uses traditional test automation for its clients, and it does improve execution speed. But it leaves the slow work untouched: teams must still create the scenarios, convert them into scripts, maintain locators and dependencies, and diagnose failures. When a linked user story changes, scripts generated for an earlier story can quickly become stale. A single generative AI prompt also doesn’t provide the control needed for a multi-stage engineering workflow. TCS therefore designed the Agentic Test Orchestrator to decompose testing into specialized tasks. Each task has its own agent, tools, validation rules, and context. A deterministic supervisor routes work, while an execution workflow controls retries, error classification, persistence, and reporting. To run these agents, TCS chose Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , a service to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. Three capabilities drove the decision. First, Amazon Bedrock offers a choice of models, so each agent uses the model that fits its task, such as scenario design or code generation, and TCS can adopt newer models as they become available. Second, AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, scales with demand, so testers across many tenants can run generation and execution sessions at the same time without TCS provisioning or tuning agent servers. Third, the runtime runs each session in its own isolated microVM, which gives TCS session-level separation for its multi-tenant platform without having to build that layer itself. Together, these capabilities let TCS focus its engineering effort on testing logic rather than agent infrastructure, which shortened the time to bring the platform to its BFSI clients. Inputs from Jira, business requirement documents (BRDs), and GitLab enter a tenant web application that runs on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) behind Amazon CloudFront , with sign-in through Amazon Cognito . TCS uses Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime to host the platform’s specialized agents, built with the Strands Agents SDK . title: Amazon Bedrock tokenomics data lake
abstract: If you need an observability data lake for your Amazon Bedrock workloads, you’re not alone. When you’re running thousands of model invocations a day across multiple accounts, after a request is sent you might be wondering, what happened? You can see the aggregate bill, but you can’t see what happened inside each call. You might start to ask questions: what prompt was sent, what the model returned, how many tokens it used, which model handled it, and whether the response was any good! If you’re a platform or machine learning (ML) engineer looking after a fleet of Amazon Bedrock workloads across teams, that’s a real problem. You can’t debug a spike, you can’t spot wasteful prompts, and you can’t tell one team’s usage from another’s. We built something to help: a centralized observability data lake for your Amazon Bedrock invocations. In this post, I cover what native data you have and how we designed the lake. I also show how to use it to see your prompts and derive the per-invocation cost. The AWS CloudFormation templates, AWS Lambda code, and SQL queries are all in the AWS Sample Bedrock Invocation Data Lake GitHub repository . This post walks through the architecture and deployment steps. The repo has everything you need to deploy it. What Amazon Bedrock visibility do you have today? Amazon Bedrock offers model invocation logging , and it’s genuinely powerful. You turn on invocation logs in the settings in each AWS account you are using Bedrock . It delivers a full record of requests and responses to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) or Amazon CloudWatch . The data exists, but it’s locked inside individual accounts. What you really want is a single, fast, queryable view of every invocation across your whole organization. That’s what the data lake gives you. What is the Amazon Bedrock observability data lake? A centralized Amazon Bedrock invocation log data lake pulls raw model invocation logs from your linked accounts into Amazon CloudWatch . Subscription log filters then forward those records to your central account. The central account processes the data through Amazon Data Firehose , and exposes them through Amazon Athena as one clean table you can query across your organization. Figure 1: Amazon Bedrock invocation observability data lake architecture across a central account and linked accounts Everything is deployed as Infrastructure as Code using two AWS CloudFormation templates, so you can roll it out repeatably across every account in your organization. This can be found in the AWS Sample Bedrock Invocation Data Lake GitHub repository . What does each Amazon Bedrock invocation log capture? After we run this solution, you will have a combined set of data across the linked account you deploy to so you can query with Athena. What you get per invocation after the logs are flattened into the processed table: The prompt the user or application sent. The model response that came back. Input and output token counts , so you can measure the true weight of each call. The model used, so you can understand utilization of models across teams. The stop reason (for example, max_tokens ), which tells you when a response was cut off. The account and timestamp , so you can attribute and time-slice everything. The AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role , so you can see who sent the prompt. After every invocation is captured like this, you go from “We used X tokens on Amazon Bedrock” to “Here is exactly what each model calls contained, and how efficient it was.” That’s the visibility platform and ML teams have been missing. title: How skills and agents work in AWS Quick
abstract: If you use AI agents, you’ve probably explained the same task more than once. You might describe how to build your weekly status update, write release notes, manage a project, or create tickets. These are all repeatable tasks that you can encode using AWS Quick through agents and skills. AWS Quick is an AI-powered service for automating tasks, analyzing data, building web applications, and conducting research. You work with it in natural language, and Quick uses AI agents to process your requests against your connected data sources and applications. In this post, we cover how agents, skills, and your data fit together in AWS Quick, and how to build and share skills that work for your team. We also show how the official catalog and custom agents help you put those skills to use. Understanding foundational concepts In this section, we explain the foundational concepts that help you understand AWS Quick in relation to agents, skills, and your data. Figure 1: How a Quick agent follows its instructions, loads the skills a task needs, acts through connectors, and grounds its answers in your data The agent sits at the center of Figure 1. It follows its instructions, loads the skills that a task calls for, takes action through connectors, and grounds its answers in your data: spaces, knowledge bases, datasets, and dashboards. Working with agents An agent in AWS Quick is a configurable AI with its own instructions, knowledge sources (spaces), and connectors, which it uses to answer questions and get work done for you. You can work with an agent in chat, or let it run on its own using a routine . Agents can only reach the resources and services that you can, and you decide what each agent is allowed to do. Quick is the default built-in agent that every user has access to. It has no fixed scope, so in each conversation it works with whatever resources you have access to, such as your spaces, knowledge bases, dashboards, connectors, and skills. You don’t need to decide in advance which data or tools a request needs, so you can start most work with Quick. A custom agent is one that you or someone on your team configures for a specific job. An example is a human resources (HR) onboarding assistant that answers new-hire questions from the HR team’s space. You give it its own instructions and limit it to the spaces, connectors, and skills that your use case requires. After you test and publish it, you can share it with other users and groups within your AWS Quick account. For a walkthrough of building one, see Build AI-powered employee onboarding agents with AWS Quick . Working with data Agents ground their answers in the data you connect to Quick. A space is a curated collection of documents and AWS Quick resources that an agent uses as a source of information. You can create one for yourself, your team, or another group in your organization. You can upload files and folders to a space, or add assets such as dashboards, knowledge bases, action connectors, and datasets. When you start a conversation with Quick, you can attach a space to narrow the data that Quick uses for that conversation. When you add a space to an agent, the space becomes part of the agent’s configuration, and the agent draws on it when a request needs it. A knowledge base is an organized, indexed collection of documents or content from data sources, optimized for retrieval and question answering. Quick syncs knowledge bases from sources such as Google Drive, Microsoft OneDrive, Confluence, Microsoft SharePoint, Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), web crawler, or Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Bases . Quick keeps them up to date on a sync schedule. Datasets and dashboards come from AWS Quick Sight , the business intelligence feature in Quick, which is available in accounts provisioned through the AWS Management Console. title: Fact-Checking at Scale: Building a More Accurate and Efficient Synopsis Factuality System
abstract: By Shreya S Ramanujam , Yongce Li , Afshine Amidi , Sina Ghiassian , Benjamin Klein . Introduction Picture this — you’re home after a long day at work and can’t wait to catch up on Bridgerton. You log on to Netflix, search for “Bridgerton” and land on this screen: If this sounds familiar, you already know what a synopsis is — it’s a short glimpse into what a viewer can expect to see in a show. We see two types of synopses here: a series-level synopsis describing the overarching plot, and multiple episode-level synopses describing each episode. A synopsis plays a very important role for us — it helps viewers decide whether a title is worth watching or not. Every synopsis needs to strike a balance: sharing just enough to give viewers a sense of what to expect, while leaving enough intrigue to draw them in. But of course, we can’t just write anything . “In the fog-drenched streets of Victorian London, Detective Daphne Bridgerton races to unmask a serial killer known only as the elusive Lady Whistledown.” Intriguing? Definitely. But it is most certainly not the premise of Bridgerton. Which leads us to the first (and most important) rule of writing a good synopsis: it must be factual . At Netflix’s scale, with thousands of titles, multiple episodes per season and multiple languages, fact-checking all of these by hand simply doesn’t scale. This is where our factuality service comes in: an automated way to judge whether a synopsis is factual or not. Our current factuality checker feeds a reasoning model everything we know about a title (like metadata and text assets) and asks it to judge synopsis factuality according to a rigorous rubric. There are two main limitations of this approach that we want to optimize: High cost of long-context reasoning calls: Each decision requires expensive, long-context model calls to reasoning models, which doesn’t scale well when we want to check multiple titles, episodes, languages, and style variants. Misaligned rationales: The model’s explanations often diverge from our annotators’ reasoning, which makes its factuality verdicts less reliable. We want these rationales to be better aligned so that (1) the model can consistently flag nuanced errors, and (2) its explanations can be used downstream to automatically correct issues in the synopsis. Our new approach tackles both problems at once. On the cost side, it delivers a 52.4% reduction per synopsis. On the quality side, it significantly improves both verdict accuracy and reasoning alignment: Recall–Fail ( “Of all truly non-factual synopses, how many does the system correctly reject?” ) rises from 0.77 to 0.86 , and the new factuality service’s explanations now show ~ 82% overlap with human rationales (up from ~ 69% ). In other words, it’s not just cheaper and more accurate — it’s also much better aligned with how our expert annotators actually judge synopses. So, what exactly does factuality mean? Let’s go back to the Bridgerton example. Say you see this synopsis about Bridgerton Season 1: Synopsis A: “Bridgerton follows Daphne Bridgerton, the eldest daughter of the powerful Bridgerton family as she makes her debut onto Regency London’s competitive marriage market.” It’s easy to judge that this synopsis is factually correct — no wrong facts, and it gives the reader a clear, accurate glimpse of what to expect from the show. Let’s take another example: Synopsis B: “Set in modern-day London, this gritty crime drama follows Detective Daphne Bridgerton as she hunts a serial killer while hiding her own criminal past.” Another easy one — the plot is so blatantly off the mark that it is definitely not factual. But what about this? Synopsis C: “Bridgerton follows the mysterious, sharp-tongued Lady Whistledown as she exposes the secrets of London’s high society through her scandalous gossip sheet.” Technically, every statement here is true — Lady Whistledown does indeed publish a gossip sheet, and if there’s one thing she is known for, it’s her scathing expos

title: Skipper, Airbnb’s embedded workflow engine, is now open source
abstract: Durable workflows, running inside your service with no separate orchestration cluster. By : Ricardo Gamba , Andriy Sergiyenko Skipper , an embedded workflow engine used in production by teams all across Airbnb, is now available to the open source community. Skipper lets you express multi-step business processes as Java or Kotlin classes, persist their progress, and recover from crashes and transient failures. It runs inside your service and reuses its existing dependencies. Skipper is available under the Apache 2.0 license. The code is on GitHub , alongside documentation and runnable examples. Our earlier engineering deep dive explains how we built it. Here, we’ll focus on the architecture of Skipper and where it fits in the ecosystem of options for development around workflows. Why we developed Skipper A process that spans multiple services, waits for human input, or involves a mix of synchronous and asynchronous steps, needs persistent storage for recording its progress. When a server restarts, it must know what has already happened, what (if anything) should be retried, and what is still awaiting processing. Implementing this separately for each process would mean repeatedly solving the same problems around partial failure, timers, and recovery, with associated testing and debugging; using a proven library is likely to improve quality and reduce toil. Existing workflow engines meet these challenges. A common approach relies on a central orchestration service, whether self-hosted or fully managed, to handle durable execution. This setup provides a unified platform for multiple teams, streamlining central operations and monitoring. For Airbnb, we wanted a new approach, one in which each service owned its workflows within its existing deployment and database. For critical services, that meant avoiding an additional shared orchestration dependency. It also let workflow execution stay in-process, without a separate coordinator between steps. That requirement shaped Skipper’s architecture, as shown in the figure. With Skipper, the service’s replicas also run the workflow runtime and scheduler. In a typical production deployment, they share a database that holds workflow state and scheduled work. The scheduler polls for runnable tasks and uses leases to coordinate ownership. If a replica fails, another can recover the work; takeover timing depends on scheduling and lease settings. This reduces the number of separately deployed systems. It also puts responsibility for workflow execution, database capacity, and recovery with the service’s team. The duty of assuming those responsibilities is part of the tradeoff. We believe that Skipper will appeal to teams that have a robust operational environment and need a workflow engine that adapts to their existing ways of working. A workflow is a class Skipper has two main abstractions. A workflow describes the orchestration: decisions, ordering, and waits. Actions perform work with potential side effects, such as calling an API or updating a database. Skipper records action results so they can be reused during recovery. Consider a hypothetical listing-publication process. Some listings require a human review before publication; afterward, the host receives a notification: class PublishListing : Workflow() { private val listing = actions<ListingActions>() @StateField var reviewApproved: Boolean? = null @WorkflowMethod suspend fun publish(request: PublicationRequest): Boolean { if (request.requiresReview) { val reviewed = waitUntil( { reviewApproved != null }, Duration.ofDays(1) ) if (!reviewed || reviewApproved != true) return false } listing.publish(request.listingId, request.requestId) listing.notifyHost(request.listingId, request.requestId) return true } @SignalMethod fun recordReview(approved: Boolean) { reviewApproved = approved } } waitUntil hibernates the workflow without holding a thread. Top News Nvidia board probes Jensen Huang alleged Chinese spy affair Sources: Nvidia will investigate CEO Jensen Huang’s relationship with possible Chinese spy Everything we know so far about the Nvidia spy scandal targeting CEO Jensen Huang The US let Nvidia sell chips to an empty office in China AI Companies Play Cat-and-Mouse With Secret-Stealing Spies OpenAI employee arrested for allegedly planting a bug in a conference room OpenAI now trains its frontier AI models with no internet access Source Nvidia’s board said Sunday it has opened an independent investigation, following reports that a Chinese intelligence operation had targeted CEO Jensen Huang. A memo circulating among US policymakers earlier this year said China’s Ministry of State Security had recruited Alice Huang to target him. She is a former executive at the Singapore-based chip firm Megaspeed, which rented access to Nvidia GPUs, and no relation to the CEO; US intelligence reports had flagged her since last year. Nvidia also published a message Huang sent to staff acknowledging an affair, without naming the woman involved. “I was unfaithful to my wife,” he wrote. “There is no excuse for what I did.” The board said it has “no reason to believe” that national security or company secrets were compromised, and that it retains confidence in Huang and his leadership team. Independent directors will run the review with outside legal counsel, and Nvidia had earlier described the pair’s interactions as “not unusual,” noting it does not share classified information with customers. The episode lands amid scrutiny of who is cleared to buy Nvidia hardware in China. Where Are the “Killer Apps” of AI?
abstract: Most of today’s AI entrepreneurs and social media enthusiasts are young. AI is the first technology revolution they’ve lived through. They don’t remember how unbelievably exciting it was in the late 1970s to get your own computer, instead of struggling to get time on one of the vast machines chugging away in what used to be called “the glass house,” an air-conditioned room where from outside you could watch the nine-track tapes being accessed and the refrigerator-sized disk drives spinning. Input and output was on high-speed teletype printers (no screens) and magnetic tape (and before that on punch cards.) They also mostly don’t remember, as I do, writing assembly-language programs in which you moved data from one computer register to another, specified the arithmetic or logical operations to be performed on it, and then specified where to save the result. They look at today’s AI and marvel at how virtually anyone can now generate code. They don’t realize that that’s also how it felt when you could use an interpreted programming language like BASIC to write your own applications instead of writing them in Assembler. They also don’t remember when Dan Bricklin used BASIC to write the first version of VisiCalc in 1979. He went into business with Bob Frankston, who rewrote it in 6502 Assembly Language for the Apple II. Dan was able to express the idea in Basic; Bob then wrote a tight, efficient version for widespread distribution. People rushed out to buy computers so they could use VisiCalc, and everyone predicted that the VisiCalc “spreadsheet” would put all the accountants out of work. It was the first program to be referred to as a “killer app.” It wasn’t the democratization of programming itself that was the killer app but what Dan and Bob did with it. In the entrepreneurial explosion that followed, databases, graphics, word processing, and other business applications came out of the glass house and, as Bill Gates put it, “onto every desk and into every home.” Dan Bricklin (right) with Bob Frankston, who rewrote VisiCalc in 6502 Assembly Language for the Apple II Image from https://www.digitec.ch/en/page/visicalc-the-first-killer-app-in-computer-history-16230 We saw the same leap from astonishment to innovation to adoption with the World Wide Web. When O’Reilly demonstrated GNN , the first commercial website, to people at a trade show in 1993, attendees couldn’t believe that clicking on a link could pop up an image or a document from another computer thousands of miles away. They didn’t understand the difference between the software application (the web browser) from the network-connected documents with clickable hyperlinks that it acted as a frame for. They didn’t understand that web pages were a new kind of software written in a simple markup language anyone could understand. It didn’t make sense that the web page was a document that in many ways could look and act like a kind of program. And when people did understand, they thought that might be the end of programming. In 1993, everyone thought that the web browser itself was the killer app, and that Marc Andreessen, the young creator of Mosaic, the most popular web browser, which became Netscape, was going to dethrone Bill Gates as the new king of computing. They didn’t realize that the true killer apps of the web were not the web browser and the web server but applications “up the stack” built using the new programming paradigm the web enabled. Those applications weren’t software as we’d known software before. They were database- and application-backed websites delivering services that were previously impossible. I remember thinking of Amazon as the 2005 equivalent to VisiCalc when a friend told me she had just bought her first computer so she could shop on Amazon. Once again, it wasn’t the new capability itself that was the killer app but what developers did with it. What makes a killer app? title: Measuring AI’s Unintended Consequences
abstract: The following article was originally published on James Shore’s Successful Software blog and is being republished here with the author’s permission. AI is great for making teams faster. But is it sustainable? What about maintainability, burnout, and lock-in? This is part 3 of my series on assessing AI’s impact on software development. In part 1 , we looked at why assessing impact is important, and what not to do. In part 2 , we looked at how to measure AI’s impact on delivery speed. In this part, we’re looking at how to measure and model the unintended consequences of using AI. Then we’ll wrap up in part 4 with an examination of business outcomes. Finally, an epilogue puts it all together with notes you can share with your CFO. Does maintainability even matter? I can hear it now: “Who cares about namby-pamby issues like maintainability and burnout? It’s a job. If jobs were supposed to be fun, they wouldn’t be called ‘work!’ Suck it up!” So let me be clear: We care about AI’s unintended consequences because they have real economic impact. If code isn’t maintainable, features take longer to write and bugs take longer to fix, taking time away from more valuable work. If people are burned out, they don’t put forth their full effort, and they eventually quit, taking institutional knowledge with them and leading to time-consuming hiring cycles. If you’re locked in, and AI token costs increase, you could be stuck with a choice between a big bill and cutting back on development. Among the people I’ve talked to, there’s widespread agreement that heavy use of AI produces code that humans have trouble understanding. But there’s disagreement about how much that matters. If AI is doing the maintenance, do we care if a human can understand the code? There are strong opinions on this topic on all sides, but not a lot of actual evidence. What’s clear is that the costs of maintenance and other unintended consequences do matter, but only if there are any costs. This is what we need to measure: Is there an impact? And if there is, is it enough to matter? Unfortunately, unlike the rigorous speed trial we discussed in part 2 , unintended consequences are gradual and fuzzy. Your measurements are going to be noisy and lagging. You’ll have to create models and explore scenarios. Ultimately, your decisions will come down to judgment, informed by your measurements and models but not driven by them. One ring to rule them all There is one idea that, while not perfect, does a good job of capturing the majority of unintended consequences. It’s cost of change . Put simply, cost of change is like a tax on the changes you make to your software. When cost of change is low, complicated changes still take time, but they’re achievable. When cost of change is high, even simple changes can take weeks, and complicated changes seem completely out of reach. Cost of change isn’t easy to measure, but there are several indicators you can use to inform your judgment. Value-add percentage Value-add percentage is the percentage of your software development effort that’s spent on things that bring value to your business, such as new features, versus the percentage of effort that’s spent on non-value-add work, such as fixing bugs, resolving incidents, and manual test and release cycles. Non-value-add work is called “muda.” 1 Some muda is necessary, even valuable, but that doesn’t make it value-add. Imagine a demanding and crotchety customer who always asks, “Why didn’t you just do it right the first time?” If that customer won’t pay for something, it’s muda. That’s why bug fixes are muda: “I’m not paying you to fix a bug that shouldn’t be there in the first place!” And performing releases: “Why don’t you just ship it already! How hard can it be?” Sure, bug fixes can be valuable, and releases are necessary, but they’re still muda. I find it useful to distinguish muda further into discretionary and nondiscretionary muda. Discretionary muda is work that you choose, such as inves

title: Human-Pilled
abstract: The following article originally appeared on the Asimov’s Addendum Substack and is being republished here with the author’s permission. This essay is based on my conversation with Demetrios Brinkmann for AAIF Live, recorded before my keynote at AGNTCon + MCPCon North America in San Jose on October 23, 2026. It was edited and rearranged for publication by Ilan Strauss, and in places it draws on the keynote. Both videos are also on the AI Disclosures Project website in the new “Missing Mechanisms” page. The keynote begins at 1:28:40 in the Day 2 livestream . The Bitter Lesson vs. AI Markets for Human Expertise In 2019, the computer scientist Richard Sutton wrote a short essay called “ The Bitter Lesson .” Looking back over 70 years of AI research, he concluded that general methods that scale with raw computation beat methods built on human expertise, and by a large margin. The AI industry as a whole is bitter-lesson-pilled, to borrow the internet’s slang for a true believer. I am human-pilled. I believe in the bitter lesson. Brute force wins out in the end, and I have wrestled with that fact throughout my career. But we humans still have to figure out our role in the AI economy, and I find it rather disturbing that the AI community isn’t spending more time asking how to make this future friendlier for humans. The labs think about how to keep AI from going rogue, and their chief economists study job losses from AI. They don’t study what mechanisms we could introduce to create new economic opportunities for humans. The question matters to us at O’Reilly Media. We don’t think of ourselves as a publisher, a conference producer, or an online learning platform so much as a company that transfers knowledge from the people at the cutting edge to the people who want to follow them. So we are very interested in what human expertise is worth, even in the face of AI. Knowing everything and nothing Human expertise was used to train AI, which makes AI a fabulous cultural technology . Thousands of years ago, the only knowledge people had was what they could keep in their heads. Since then we have built better and better ways to share knowledge across time and space, and AI continues that. With each of these transitions, we have to ask again what the truly human is still worth. People often say judgment, or taste. That’s true, but I think it goes deeper: AI is a sea of possibility. All of that knowledge sits in the model, and nothing sets it in motion except a human. (That is changing a little as we start giving AI agents long-running tasks, and we will have to come to grips with it.) If you and I used Claude or ChatGPT for the same research project, we would each bring different experience to it, tell it what we want and why, and give it context in different ways. I see that as the unique focusing power of human consciousness and attention. Earlier this year I spent an hour or so talking this question over with Claude. When it offered to write up a first draft for me, I said no. I wanted an essay from its own point of view about what it took away from our conversation. The result, “ Why AI Needs Us ,” opens, “He came in through Powys,” and a few paragraphs later says, “The choice of entry point was already the argument.” That captured what I’m getting at. I had come into the conversation through a book I love, John Cowper Powys’s The Meaning of Culture , which distinguishes culture from education. Powys gives his own unique and powerful definition: “Culture is what is left over after you have forgotten all you have definitely set out to learn.” It is what you absorbed. Each of us absorbs a small and particular slice of everything. Large language models (LLMs) try to absorb everything, and so become overly general; we give them focus. Human knowledge provides them with a lens. Let me bring that into a business context. title: Why AI Agents Are Repeating 2019’s Microservices Mistake
abstract: Microservices changed how we build software by breaking large applications into smaller, independently deployable services. That made systems easier to develop and scale, but it introduced a different class of problems: The behavior of the whole system got harder to see. AI agents are now following a similar path. A workflow that once lived inside a single application gets split across several agents, each responsible for one task. Individual pieces may work exactly as designed while the overall workflow gradually produces worse results. The difference is that agents make these systems far faster and cheaper to create, which makes it easier to repeat the same architectural mistake at a much larger scale. I learned this the hard way. My name was on the design doc. Splitting that workflow across three agents was a reasonable call, and I would still defend most of the reasoning. But if you’d asked me that afternoon how we would find out when the thing quietly stopped working, I had no answer. Months later, in a quality review, a reviewer noticed something felt off before any of our instrumentation caught it. Latency looked fine, error rates were flat, and every service in the chain returned what it was supposed to return. What we had was a slow decline in output quality, and it took about three weeks to trace. The first agent handed a set of documents to the next one for summarization. The summarizer dropped a field it had judged to be a low signal. A downstream agent then made a confident recommendation without that field. Every agent did what it had been designed to do, and the result was still wrong. I should have anticipated it, because I’d been on the product side through the microservices years and had seen this pattern before. The hangover we already paid for Breaking down monoliths was a good decision for most teams, but one thing was forgotten. Decomposition did not make the difficult parts of the system disappear. It moved them into the gaps between services, where the people accountable for the overall product could no longer see them. The bill landed around 2019, and it landed on the delivery schedule rather than the incident channel. Teams were running hundreds of services with limited tracing and no contract versioning, and the real symptom was slower delivery. Shipping took longer than before, because engineers spent their weeks picking through those services. Agents are running the same arc faster, because standing one up takes an afternoon and a prompt instead of a repo and a deploy pipeline. When creating an agent is that cheap, product teams make agents without asking anyone, and nobody keeps track of what the agents are and what they’re doing. What breaks, and what it costs you This isn’t only my experience. Cemri and coauthors annotated more than 1,600 execution traces across seven popular multi-agent frameworks and built a taxonomy of 14 recurring failure modes ( MAST , NeurIPS 2025). Most of what goes wrong traces back to how the system was specified and how its agents coordinated, not to the models inside it. Inventory sounds trivial and isn’t. Service sprawl at least showed up in your Kubernetes manifests. Agents get created inside product surfaces and workflow tools, and inside somebody’s weekend automation of their own job. You don’t find out what you have until a compliance reviewer asks which automated system touched a given decision, and then it’s too late. The visibility gap cost us three weeks. When an agent calls an agent that calls a retrieval layer that calls another agent, and every hop has a model deciding what to pass forward, you need trace context that survives the whole path. Most stacks log prompts and completions per call and stop there. You get each hop and never the chain, and it was the chain that failed. Compounding confidence is the failure that worries me most. title: What to know about this year’s UN climate talks
abstract: It’s that time of year again: Thousands of delegates, lobbyists, and journalists are gathered for the annual UN climate talks, taking place this time in Antalya, Turkey. COP31 officially kicked off on November 8, marking the beginning of negotiations on one of the biggest stages of the climate world. Turkey and Australia are cohosting this year’s talks, which are scheduled to wrap up on November 20. This annual gathering can often serve as an indicator of where the world stands on addressing and adapting to the climate crisis. And this year’s talks are sure to be a doozy—expect a lot of back and forth on fossil fuels and climate finance in particular. Here’s what you should know about COP31. In recent years, the tension always feels high when COP rolls around. (COP stands for “Conference of the Parties.”) But this year feels especially charged: The world is still grappling with the ongoing war in Iran, which has disrupted the Middle East and sent economic shock waves around the world as energy prices have spiked. This year’s COP will be the second without a formal delegation from the US. President Trump formally withdrew the country from the Paris Agreement earlier this year and is in the process of withdrawing from the UN Framework Committee on Climate Change. That’s the treaty that allows formal participation in negotiations. Meanwhile, things aren’t looking good for the Paris Agreement, which was established at UN climate talks 11 years ago, setting a goal of limiting warming to 1.5 °C over preindustrial levels. In a report published in September, the UN Environment Program acknowledged that global warming is set to exceed that 1.5 °C goal, “likely within the next few years.” So as climate talks kick off, there’s an obvious, urgent question looming about how to quickly cut emissions to limit warming. There’s also the major issue of how to pay for efforts to address emissions and to help a warming world endure the inevitable damage. Two years ago, talks ended in a goal of mobilizing $300 billion per year by 2035 to help pay to reduce emissions and adapt to climate change. (Rich nations provided $136.7 billion in 2024, according to the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development. ) And last year, the COP30 agreement included a goal of tripling the money for adaptation over that period. (Such funding has been quite flat over the past few years.) The world got a tragic reminder of just how high the stakes are earlier this year, when a glacier collapse caused devastating flooding in the Himalayas. The flood killed approximately 1,500 people, left over 5,000 missing, and caused nearly $5 billion in damage. The UN loss and damages fund committed $20 million to helping Nepal recover (less than 1% of the total estimated cost to the country). Another key trend to watch is how the formal negotiations engage with the topic of fossil fuels. Three years ago, the final agreement text explicitly called for a transition away from them. But it felt as if things took a step back last year, when the final agreement didn’t even mention the phrase “fossil fuels” once. This will be an interesting conversation, especially because cohosts Turkey and Australia have both faced criticism over their relationships with these fuels—Australia is a major exporter of coal and natural gas, and Turkey’s grid relies heavily on fossil fuels, including coal. Outside the formal negotiations, COP31 president Murat Kurum, Turkey’s environment minister, is spearheading a side agenda, including two informal initiatives that will be worth watching. These wouldn’t be part of the official agreement text, but countries could sign on to signal support. One is a pledge to make AI more sustainable; this is almost comically squishy, even as voluntary COP pledges go. The text includes explicit wording that it creates no new obligations for countries, so don’t expect anything resembling enforcement there. title: The Download: preserving minds and weighing open AI risks
abstract: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. Six wild ideas for perpetuating your mind As we age, we forget most of what we’ve experienced, yet there’s still undeniable continuity: At 30, or 50, or 70, you will still be you. To preserve that elusive continuity of self, some far-thinking technologists are exploring ways to keep the brain going, even beyond death. Their ideas range from freezing brains in liquid nitrogen to augmenting living ones and uploading our memories to the cloud. Here are six possible paths for keeping your mind going, and how feasible they might be . —Antonio Regalado This story is from the Impossible edition of our print magazine. Subscribe now to get every issue as soon as it lands. MIT Technology Review Narrated: Open models have real benefits. Do they outweigh the risks? title: Evolving metal extraction processes
abstract: The metals industry has experienced transformational moments before: the Bessemer process, flash smelting, electric arc furnaces, and modern continuous casting all changed what was possible. Yet, for more than a century, most extraction processes rely on techniques and pathways that would be familiar to metallurgists from generations ago. Processes have become larger and control systems smarter, but the fundamental science behind separating metals from ores has changed less than many realize. Today’s materials challenges are different from those of the 20th century, but why are critical metals still produced using largely the same scientific foundations? EvoMaterials, a technology platform developed by Outokumpu—the global leader in sustainable stainless steel and the producer of ferrochrome with 67% lower carbon footprint than the industry average—is exploring that question by rethinking how metals can be extracted: “We decided to go beyond the current constraints and look fundamentally at what’s the best way to do this with the benefit of the scientific engineering knowledge and hindsight that we have today,” says Caspar Stinn, technical director for extractive metallurgy at Outokumpu. “We’re looking at how we can reimagine metals production.” A supply chain problem disguised as a materials problem As economies expand and the world becomes increasingly electrified, data and scientific models point to rising demand for many minerals, driven by technologies ranging from data centers to aerospace, water treatment, energy systems, and defence. According to Antoine Allanore, professor of metallurgy at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) this coincides with many Western economies having reduced their domestic processing capacity for the very metals those industries depend on. Metallurgy is now strategically important, shaped not only by cost and availability but also by carbon footprint, geographic origin and supply-chain resilience. That reality is particularly relevant for chromium and other specialty metals used in high-temperature and extreme environments. Chromium-based materials play a critical role in aerospace systems, power generation, corrosion-resistant infrastructure and defense technologies, where materials must perform under demanding conditions. Beyond optimization For decades, metallurgical innovation largely focused on improving yields, energy efficiency and process control. EvoMaterials is based on the idea that some metallurgical processes may benefit from entirely different chemical pathways. The platform originates from research into sulfidation-based processing technologies, initially pursued to reduce carbon emissions associated with ferrochrome production. Laboratory work revealed broader potential. Lab-scale trials demonstrated that these alternative process chemistries could potentially do more than lower emissions. They could recover valuable metals from lower grade resources and industrial side streams while fundamentally altering how separation processes are performed. The opportunity is to rethink how mineral resources are used and how much value can be extracted from them, bringing in greater resource efficiency and stronger industrial competitiveness. title: The backlash about data centers might really just be about electricity
abstract: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here . As voters went to the polls across the US last week, I was in Ashburn, Virginia, part of what’s known as Data Center Alley—the world’s largest data center hub. It’s also where the backlash now sweeping the country arguably first began taking shape. Driving through it is surreal. Concrete monolithic buildings loom along every major road, with names like Skybox and CloudHQ. It’s accepted wisdom in Big Tech that the war against data centers must be about something bigger than just data centers themselves. Two days after the midterms, OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer, Chris Lehane, wrote that data centers “have become a proxy for public unease about affordability, corporate power, and people losing control over their futures.” It’s a culture war, in other words. But spending a few days in Data Center Alley left me wondering if it’s really the proxy that Lehane describes. I came away convinced that the data center backlash is more about electricity than Big Tech admits. The industry can improve its image, but it can’t escape the physical consequences of its enormous appetite for electricity. Here’s why. There are two ways to power the sort of data center that AI companies want: connecting to the grid, or generating electricity onsite. In Virginia’s Loudoun County, where data centers are ubiquitous but have been built at a steadier pace than the breakneck expansion now underway elsewhere in the country, most are connected to the existing grid. One facility I went inside, operated by Equinix, has massive diesel generators onsite for backup but gets its power from the local utility, Dominion Energy. Much of Dominion’s electricity is generated by natural gas (which is cleaner than coal or oil, but worse than renewables). The average data center operating in this part of Virginia today has a power capacity of 54 megawatts. That’s more than the power draw of the Denver International Airport . Elena Schlossberg, a prominent activist against data centers in Virginia, told me she’s “always banging my head against the wall” when the industry paints the fight as a culture war. “It was always about power,” she says—that is, electricity. Some Virginia protesters appear more animated by a broader anti-tech populism than Schlossberg, to be fair. But it’s the particular consequences of drawing so much power from the grid that have done the most to shape how the backlash has played out. Recent protests have led to new rules from the state that data centers must pay fully for the cost of new transmission lines to the grid and make sure they’re not spread among everyone else. Data center developers told me they’re preparing for new rules that would cut them off from grid power during peak demand. Schlossberg also worries about the downstream effects of a strained grid—for example, that data centers will run more diesel generators or that Dominion Energy will expand fossil fuel inputs rather than renewables to meet demand. The overwhelming majority of AI data centers being built elsewhere in the country are not designed this way. The scale desired is so massive that companies are setting up in rural areas where there is virtually no grid infrastructure to connect to. Building there means bringing your own power (so-called “behind the meter” power), in the form of natural-gas-powered turbines. Companies also build diesel generators for backup. Anthropic, for example, has reportedly agreed to pay $3.4 billion for gas turbines in what’s described as the largest power generation purchase by an AI company. Even if grids were nearby, they’d be unlikely to serve the amount of power demanded. The smallest data centers attractive for AI training are 300 megawatts. title: Nancy Pelosi’s replacement is ready to regulate AI
abstract: As a California state senator, Scott Wiener authored legislation aimed at curbing the risks of advanced AI. Now, after winning a tight congressional race for former Speaker of the House Nancy Pelosi’s open San Francisco seat, he could play a key role in setting federal AI policy. I spoke with Wiener on Friday, only a few hours after he had been declared the victor. But he was already thinking about AI risk. The previous day, the AI nonprofit METR had released a report that had been widely interpreted as evidence that Anthropic had achieved recursive self-improvement, a phenomenon in which AI meaningfully contributes to its own advancement and AI progress potentially spins out of control. “It’s very concerning,” Wiener said, citing the report as evidence that we are quickly running out of time to regulate AI. “It was my hope that Congress would take decisive action before [the end of] this year,” he said. “That does not appear to be happening.” Wiener has been increasingly focused on AI in recent years, and he’s made many of the AI safety movement’s concerns his own: During our 20-minute conversation, he used the phrase “recursive self-improvement” half a dozen times, for example.“We need to slow this down,” he says. “Because it’s moving very quickly, and we could sleepwalk into a disaster.” Wiener has already had real influence on AI policy. SB 1047, a bill that he authored in 2024, was set to become the first real piece of frontier AI legislation in the country before it was vetoed by California governor Gavin Newsom; he then sponsored SB 53, a lighter-touch bill that Newsom signed. Both bills have inspired proposed federal legislation. Wiener’s congressional campaign received over $3 million from Public First Action, a nonprofit in favor of AI regulation that receives substantial funding from Anthropic. That contribution led opponents to criticize him for being too close to the AI industry , but Wiener says that couldn’t be further from the truth. “Public First supported me because I was the first lawmaker in the country to introduce AI regulation and the first to pass it and get it implemented,” he wrote in a message after our interview. “The attacks on me for [Public First’s] support were shockingly cynical—literally attacking a candidate who actually regulated AI over Big Tech’s objection and falsely claiming the candidate is somehow too close to Big Tech.” Wiener says that if Congress forms a select committee on artificial intelligence—something that Democrats have discussed since September—he’d be eager to serve. And he’s enthusiastic about many of the policy ideas floating around Congress. “I think it’s really important to have a strong, empowered, nimble federal regulator,” he says, noting that Representative Ro Khanna, a fellow Democrat from California, has proposed legislation to establish such a regulator. He also highlights the importance of whistleblower protections, testing and auditing requirements, and a kill switch requirement, and he wants to see Congress leverage its oversight powers to hold the AI labs to account. “This is about the future of humanity, and we want to make sure that the public has a say and that the public knows what’s going on,” he says. And as a longtime state legislator, he is opposed to broad federal preemption of state AI laws, which some of the proposed federal legislation would require. “States are, as Brandeis says , laboratories,” he notes. “You want the states to be able to continue to be nimble in ways that Congress sometimes is not.” Above all, Wiener says, he wants Congress to pass policies with real teeth. “It’s critically important that when Congress acts, that we do so in a way that is truly meaningful and that meets the moment,” he says. title: The Download: empty AI climate claims, and an Nvidia investigation
abstract: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. Opinion: The climate case for AI has not been made —By Mary Nichols, distinguished counsel at the UCLA School of Law and the former chair of the California Air Resources Board, and Jeremy Tamanini, the founder of Dual Citizen, a sustainability research and advisory firm This week, as countries meet in Antalya, Turkey for the United Nations climate conference, one topic is likely to dominate the conversation: artificial intelligence. The host has already called on countries to commit to ensuring that AI is designed, powered, and deployed in ways that support climate action. But so far, industries around the world aren’t doing nearly enough to harness the technology to actually drive down the greenhouse-gas emissions heating up the planet. AI companies like to make very optimistic claims about AI’s potential to help address climate change. The reality is far less promising. Read the full story . Meet the ecologist revealing the invisible networks that revive rainforests Tropical forests are our planet’s biggest terrestrial carbon sink, accounting for around 40% of carbon stored on land. Forest ecologist Daisy Dent, a senior scientist at ETH Zurich, is part of an international network of researchers working to decipher the networks of animal and plant interactions that enable some forests to recover after destruction. The goal is a low-cost, high-impact alternative to typical carbon-­crediting schemes, which plant huge areas with a single species of tree. For over a decade, her research has helped show that these large “monocrop” programs could be expensive mistakes—and that more resilient forests can rebound naturally in just a few decades, re-creating ecosystems that suck up vast quantities of carbon dioxide. title: Innovating with AI in the special chemicals industry
abstract: As companies look to accelerate innovation with artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and advanced modeling, the primary challenge is connecting new technologies to reliable data, scientific expertise, and the practical realities of bringing products to market. For specialty chemicals manufacturer Lubrizol, digital transformation is all about giving researchers the tools to test ideas faster, make better-informed decisions, and develop more sustainable materials without compromising performance. Girish Rao, vice president of information technology at Lubrizol, says the company is building a digital foundation that connects business processes, modern data platforms, and cloud infrastructure to support its research and development (R&D) teams. Their goal is to combine decades of accumulated technical data with the deep expertise of chemists and engineers who understand customer needs as well as the physical constraints of their work. Data scientists can help identify patterns, test new hypotheses, and model possibilities before researchers conduct physical experiments. But, Rao emphasizes, “it’s not about replacing scientific judgment; it is about giving our scientists better tools.” Scientists, data scientists, and IT teams approach problems from different perspectives, prioritizing experimental validity, model performance, and platform security and scalability, respectively. By bringing these groups together in “fusion teams,” Lubrizol aligns them around shared objectives, starting with small pilots to build trust. “Once the trust is built between the team members and they know what value they’re about to create,” Rao says, “things go a lot better.” Cloud infrastructure also gives the company flexibility to access computing resources and modern tools without making the substantial investments required to build and maintain its own data centers. These capabilities could prove especially valuable in advancing sustainability. Digital modeling can help researchers evaluate more formulations, explore materials such as starch and corn-based alternatives, and assess trade-offs across a product’s life cycle. Promising a material in a laboratory is only the first step. Scaling production while meeting performance expectations, regulatory requirements, and financial constraints is still a tightrope walk, but AI’s ability to model multiple variables could help teams navigate those competing demands. Looking to the future, Rao expects AI, automation, advanced modeling, digital twins, and connected data to converge as laboratories become more intelligent and manufacturing plants more efficient. The opportunity, he suggests, lies in bringing these capabilities together responsibly and at scale. “It’s not just a single technology. I think it’s the combination of all of these, and it’ll be the ability to connect all these processes that are going to generate tremendous amounts of data.” This webcast is produced in partnership with Infosys. This content was produced by Insights, MIT Technology Review’s custom content arm, not its editorial staff. It was researched and written by humans, with any AI tools that may have been used limited to production processes under human oversight.

title: The climate case for AI has not been made
abstract: This week, as countries meet in Antalya, Turkey for the United Nations climate conference, one topic likely to dominate the conversation is artificial intelligence. The host has already called on countries to commit to ensuring that AI is designed, powered, and deployed in ways that support climate action. But so far, industries around the world aren’t doing nearly enough to harness the technology to actually drive down the greenhouse-gas emissions heating up the planet, despite some very optimistic claims from AI companies. In 2024, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman declared that AI would unleash “astounding triumphs,” including “fixing the climate.” The year before, in a 2023 op-ed , the head of sustainability at Google and her coauthor wrote that AI could reduce global emissions 5% to 10% by 2030. Some academic researchers have examined these AI-related climate claims. A peer-reviewed study published last year, led by researchers at the London School of Economics’ Grantham Research Institute and the firm Systemiq, estimated that AI could help cut global emissions by the equivalent of 3.2 to 5.4 billion tons of carbon dioxide annually by 2035—roughly on par with the US’s annual energy-related emissions on the high end, even after subtracting AI’s own energy footprint. Those potential gains are mostly concentrated in three sectors: power, meat and dairy, and vehicles. But projections like these are only as good as our willingness to test them against present-day reality. So is there evidence that the largest companies in these three sectors are beginning to integrate AI in line with the study’s projections, and if so, do the results match expectations? Or is the 2035 number still mostly aspirational? Companies across these sectors have announced plenty of initial efforts to incorporate AI into various business practices. But an AI-assisted review of public information from significant market actors in each sector, conducted and reviewed by the second author of this piece, found that few have announced they’re pursuing the specific emissions-reducing routes that informed the projections in the study—and fewer still claim they’ve used them to achieve meaningful climate progress. The power sector is where the earlier study’s underlying math is most concrete: AI-driven forecasting of supply and demand could increase the amount of renewable electricity that reaches the grid from already-built solar and wind facilities by up to 20%, which could prevent an estimated 1.8 billion tons of emissions a year. Yet of the grid operators reviewed in China, the United States, and Europe, only one deployed a known meaningful, working AI program of this sort, according to the analysis. A partnership between the UK’s National Grid ESO and Open Climate Fix halved the grid operator’s solar-forecast error (the difference between the amount of incoming sunlight predicted and the amount that actually reaches solar panels), avoiding hundreds of thousands of tons of carbon dioxide a year. Beyond this example in the UK, though, many other grid operators in the EU, the US, and China had little to show in the public record in terms of the AI integration envisioned by the study. The meat and dairy sector offers the starkest contrast between technology readiness and market reality. To achieve the 2035 emission reductions anticipated in the earlier study, AI would need to close the taste and cost gap between traditional proteins and alternative ones, such as lab-grown or plant-based burgers and milk substitutes. In one of the clearest efforts to achieve this, the AI and food tech company NotCo recently formed a joint venture with Kraft Heinz using its platform Giuseppe , which analyzes plant molecular data to pinpoint combinations replicating the taste, texture, and smell of animal products.
